title: Fusion music, including bhangra and reggaeton

tips.title: Both traditions have to stay audible
tips.body: A fusion brings two or more distinct styles together **so that each one can still be heard**. If one has swallowed the other you have a style, not a fusion. And if they take turns rather than sounding together, you have a medley.

tips.title: Name the tradition each feature comes from
tips.body: The single most common way to lose marks here is to say a piece "mixes two kinds of music". Say **dhol, from Punjabi folk** and **four on the floor, from Western dance music**. Every feature you name should carry its passport.

tips.title: Percussion is usually the fastest clue
tips.body: Hand and stick drums travel with their traditions and keep their own sound: **dhol** and **tabla** from South Asia, **congas** and **bongos** from Cuba, **djembe** from West Africa, **bodhrán** from Ireland. Identify the drums and you have half the fusion already.

tips.title: A drone is not a chord sequence
tips.body: Many traditions hold a single note or interval under everything instead of changing chords. That is a **drone**, and it is a different observation from harmony. Saying "the harmony does not change" misses the point: there may be no functional harmony there at all.

steps.title: What a fusion is, and what it is not
steps.body:
**Fusions** is one of Edexcel's four areas of study. Appendix 3 of the specification defines fusion as *the blending of more than one musical style or culture to create a new fused sound*.

The working definition to carry into the exam is slightly sharper:

> A fusion brings together **two or more distinct traditions** so that **each one remains audible**.

Both halves of that do work.

- **Together, not in turn.** If a track plays one style and then another, it is a **medley**. A fusion has them sounding at the same time.
- **Audible, not absorbed.** If one tradition has swallowed the other so completely that you cannot hear it, the result is a style rather than a fusion.

The pack's two Fusions set works both pass that test. Afro Celt Sound System's *Release* has West African, Celtic and Western studio elements playing at once. Esperanza Spalding's *Samba em Prelúdio* is a **bossa nova**, and bossa nova is itself Brazilian **samba** crossed with American **jazz**.

And fusion is not a modern invention. Appendix 3 defines **jazz** as *originally a fusion of African and North American styles*. A great deal of the music anybody listens to is a fusion that has been around long enough to stop sounding like one.

props.title: Four fusions, and what each one joins

visuals.alt: A table of four fusion styles with the two musical traditions each one brings together

boxes.title: A fusion
boxes.body: Two traditions sounding at the same time, both still recognisable. A dhol under a dance beat.

boxes.title: A medley
boxes.body: One style, then another. Both are there, but never at once, so nothing is fused.

boxes.title: A style
boxes.body: A fusion that settled. Jazz began as one and is now simply jazz.

boxes.title: An arrangement
boxes.body: One piece rewritten for different forces. New instruments, but only one tradition.

visuals.alt: Four boxes distinguishing a fusion from a medley, a settled style and an arrangement

check.prompt: A track plays two minutes of Irish fiddle music, then two minutes of hip hop, then returns to the fiddle. Is it a fusion?
options: Yes, because two distinct traditions are both present
Yes, because it returns to the first tradition at the end
No, because Irish music and hip hop are too far apart
No, the traditions take turns rather than sounding together
check.solution: A fusion has its traditions sounding **at the same time**. Playing one and then the other is a **medley**. Nothing about the distance between two traditions stops them fusing — Afro Celt Sound System joins West African, Celtic and Western studio music in a single texture.

steps.title: Bhangra: Punjabi folk meeting Western pop
steps.body:
**Bhangra** began as a Punjabi folk tradition — dance music associated with the harvest, sung in Punjabi and played on the instruments of the region. From the 1980s, musicians in Britain and elsewhere began setting it against Western pop, dance and hip hop production, and the fused style spread worldwide.

**The Punjabi side.**

- The **dhol**: a large double-headed barrel drum, hung from the shoulder and struck with two sticks — a thin one on the treble head and a thicker, bent one on the bass head. It is loud, outdoor music and it sounds like it.
- The **tumbi**: a single-stringed plucked instrument with a very high, bright, twanging tone, usually playing a short repeated pattern.
- The **chimta**: a long steel tong with jingles, struck to add a metallic edge.
- The **dholak** and **tabla** for finer patterns.
- Vocals in **Punjabi**, often in a call-and-response between a lead singer and a group.
- Melodies frequently **pentatonic** or modal, and often over a **drone** rather than changing chords.

**The Western side.**

- A **drum machine** or sampled kit under the dhol, often with **four on the floor**.
- **Synthesiser** pads and bass.
- **Sampling**, **looping** and studio effects — reverb, delay, filtering.
- Verse-and-chorus structure, and sometimes rapped verses from hip hop.

The fusion is easy to hear because the two percussion sounds are so different: the dhol is a struck skin with a long, woody decay, and the drum machine is a short electronic click that never varies. Put them in the same bar and neither disappears.

a single string, very high and twanging
call and response between soloist and group

steps.title: Reggaeton: the dembow, and where it comes from
steps.body:
**Reggaeton** grew up in Puerto Rico and Panama through the 1990s, out of Jamaican **dancehall** reggae, Latin American music and North American **hip hop**. It is usually in **Spanish**, usually built on a repeating chord loop, and it is defined by one rhythm above everything else.

**The dembow.** A repeating one-bar pattern whose accents fall in a **3 + 3 + 2** grouping of the 8 quavers in a four-four bar.

Count the quavers of the bar as 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &. The accents land on quavers 1, 4, 7 — that is, on **beat 1**, on the **&** between beats 2 and 3, and on **beat 4**.

That middle accent is the whole thing. One of the three lands **off the beat**, so the pattern is **syncopated**, and because it repeats every bar without variation the syncopation becomes the pulse rather than a disturbance to it. It is the same underlying grouping that runs through a great deal of Caribbean and Latin American music, which is why reggaeton feels related to styles it did not come from.

**The rest of the style.**

- A **kick drum** and **snare or rim** playing the dembow, usually sampled rather than played.
- A **repeating chord loop**, very often in a minor key.
- **Rapped and sung vocals**, alternating, in Spanish.
- Melodies that are short and heavily **syncopated** against the pattern.
- **Sampling** and looping throughout, from the hip hop side.

**Where each part comes from.** The dembow rhythm arrives from Jamaican dancehall; the rapping and the sample-based production from hip hop; the language, the melodic style and much of the percussion colour from Latin America. Three traditions, and all three audible at once.

visuals.alt: A table of the eight quavers in a four-four bar showing which three carry the accents of the dembow pattern

visuals.problem: Why does a 3 + 3 + 2 pattern sound syncopated?

steps.text: A four-four bar holds 4 crotchets, which is 8 quavers.
steps.note: Everything below counts in quavers, because the accents do not all land on crotchets.

steps.text: Grouping them 3 + 3 + 2 puts accents on quavers 1, 4, 7.
steps.note: 3 + 3 + 2 is 8, so the grouping exactly fills the bar and can repeat forever.

steps.text: Quavers 1, 3, 5 and 7 are the four beats; quavers 2, 4, 6 and 8 are the off-beats.
steps.note: An accent on an odd-numbered quaver is on a beat; on an even-numbered one it is between beats.

steps.text: The middle accent lands on quaver 4, which is off the beat.
steps.note: Exactly 1 of the three accents is off the beat. That single displacement is what gives the pattern its lean.

check.prompt: A dembow pattern groups the quavers of a four-four bar as 3 + 3 + 2. How many quavers are there in the bar altogether?
check.solution: Four-four holds 4 crotchets and a crotchet is two quavers, so the bar holds **8** quavers. The grouping has to add to that exactly, and 3 + 3 + 2 does, which is why the pattern can repeat bar after bar without drifting.

steps.title: Harmony, melody and texture in a fusion
steps.body:
**Harmony often stops moving.** Many traditions outside Western classical music do not organise themselves around changing chords at all. Instead you get one of these:

- A **drone**: a note or an interval, usually the tonic or a perfect fifth, sustained or repeated under everything. Common in South Asian and Celtic music.
- A **repeating chord loop**: two to four chords, round and round, never resolving anywhere.
- A **ground bass** or ostinato holding the bottom.

All three do the same job: they take the harmony out of the conversation so that the rhythm and the melody can carry it. Saying *the harmony does not change* misses the point; say **drone** or **loop**, and then say what that frees up.

**Melody is often pentatonic or modal.** A **pentatonic** scale has five notes — degrees 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 of a major scale — and no semitone steps anywhere in it. With no semitones there is no leading note pulling towards the tonic, so a pentatonic melody can circle indefinitely without ever needing a cadence. That suits music built over a drone exactly.

**Texture: two words that matter here.**

- **Heterophony** — two or more parts playing **the same** melody at the same time, with small variations between them. A singer decorating a line while a flute plays it plainly is heterophonic, and this texture is common in fusions and rare in the Western classical set works.
- **Call and response** — a phrase in one part answered by a phrase in another. It comes from oral traditions in West Africa and South Asia among many others, and Appendix 3 defines **oral tradition** as music learnt by listening and repeating.

**The studio is a tradition too.** Loops, **sampling**, reverb, delay and filtering are Western studio practice, and in a fusion they are an ingredient rather than packaging. Afro Celt Sound System's *Release* uses the studio as deliberately as it uses the kora.

rows: a held note or fifth under everything
two to four chords repeating unchanged
Baroque music, and much else since

check.prompt: A synthesiser holds one low note for an entire track while the melody moves above it. What should you call that note?
options: A chord loop
A ground bass
A pedal cadence
A drone
check.solution: A **drone**: a note, or an interval such as a perfect fifth, sustained or repeated under the music. A chord loop would need chords that change; a ground bass is a repeating bass *pattern* rather than one held note; "pedal cadence" is not a term at all.

steps.title: The percussion of four traditions
steps.body:
Drums travel with their traditions and keep their own sound, so identifying the percussion usually identifies the fusion. These are the ones worth knowing by name.

**South Asia**

- **Dhol** — a large double-headed barrel drum, struck with two sticks. Loud, outdoor, the sound of bhangra.
- **Dholak** — smaller, played with the hands, for finer patterns.
- **Tabla** — a pair of tuned hand drums, capable of enormously intricate patterns and of bending pitch.

**The Caribbean and Latin America**

- **Congas** — tall single-headed hand drums, in sets of two or three.
- **Bongos** — a joined pair of small, high hand drums.
- **Timbales** — shallow metal-shelled drums played with sticks, with cowbells attached.
- **Claves** — two hardwood sticks struck together, cutting through everything and usually holding the pattern the rest of the band plays against.

**West Africa**

- **Djembe** — a goblet-shaped hand drum with a wide range of tone from centre to edge.
- **Talking drum** — an hourglass drum whose tension, and therefore pitch, changes as the player squeezes the cords.

**Ireland and Scotland**

- **Bodhrán** — a shallow frame drum played with a double-ended beater.

And from the Western studio: the **drum kit**, the **drum machine**, and the **sampled loop**, which is a recording of a drum rather than a drum.

A fusion often puts one of these against another. When it does, that pairing is the most concrete evidence you have, so name both drums and both traditions.

rows: two sticks, one on each head
a double-ended beater on a frame drum

Dhol against a drum machine
Djembe against a talking drum
Bodhran against a fiddle
check.solution: The **dhol** is Punjabi and the **drum machine** is Western studio equipment, so hearing them in the same bar is two traditions at once. The other three pairs are each two instruments from the *same* tradition, so none of them is evidence of a fusion at all.

steps.title: A fusion extract, worked
steps.body:
Here is an extract described as an exam would present it. Work through it the way a fusion question wants: name the traditions, then attach every feature to one of them.

**On the page:** one sharp in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a fast tempo.

**What you hear:**

- A synthesiser holds a low G under the whole extract, never changing.
- A dhol plays a repeating one-bar pattern, struck with sticks.
- Under the dhol, a bass drum lands on all four beats and never varies by a hair.
- A tumbi plays a short, very high, twanging pattern, repeated without change.
- A voice sings in Punjabi, using only the notes G, A, B, D and E.
- A second group of voices answers each of the solo voice's phrases.
- A sampled string chord appears at the start of each eight-bar section, clearly lifted from another recording.

The working below takes it apart.

visuals.problem: Name the traditions in this extract, and give two features from each.

steps.text: The traditions are Punjabi folk and Western pop and dance.
steps.note: Name them first. Every point afterwards attaches to one of the two, which is what a fusion answer is marked on.

steps.text: From Punjabi folk: the dhol, the tumbi, and the Punjabi vocals.
steps.note: All three are specific instruments or practices of the tradition, not general descriptions.

steps.text: Also from the folk side: the call and response between the solo voice and the group.
steps.note: Appendix 3 defines oral tradition as music learnt by listening and repeating; call and response belongs to that world rather than to notation.

steps.text: From Western pop and dance: the four on the floor bass drum, and the synthesiser drone.
steps.note: The bass drum on all four beats came in with disco. A synthesiser is electronic and belongs to the studio side.

steps.text: Also Western: the sampled string chord, and the fact that the beat never varies.
steps.note: Sampling is studio practice, and machine-perfect timing means a sequencer rather than a player.

steps.text: The five notes G, A, B, D and E are the G major pentatonic.
steps.note: Degrees 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 of G major, with no semitone anywhere, so the melody never pulls towards a cadence.

steps.text: The held G is a drone, not a harmony.
steps.note: With one note underneath and a pentatonic melody above, there is tonality but no functional harmony, which is what lets the two traditions sit together.

check.solution: **Pentatonic**. Those five notes are degrees 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 of G major, and the specification defines a pentatonic scale in exactly that way. There is no semitone step anywhere in it, so the melody has no leading note pulling towards the tonic and can circle over a drone indefinitely without needing a cadence.

steps.title: Why fusions happen
steps.body:
A fusion answer that only lists ingredients stops at the middle of the mark scheme. What lifts it is saying **why** the two traditions are together, and **what the fusion achieves that neither could alone**.

**People move, and take their music with them.** Bhangra fused with Western pop largely in Britain, among Punjabi communities, because both musics were in the same rooms. Reggaeton grew where Jamaican, Latin American and North American music were all being heard at once. The geography is part of the explanation.

**Technology makes it easy.** Once a rhythm can be **sampled** and looped, a producer can put a dhol pattern under a dance beat without a dhol player being present. Sampling did not create fusion, but it made it cheap.

**The two traditions do different jobs.** In most successful fusions, each tradition supplies something the other does not have. A drone gives a floor with no harmonic argument, which frees a Western beat to be simple and relentless. A pentatonic melody never demands a cadence, so it can sit over a loop that never resolves. Neither tradition has to give anything up.

**And sometimes it is about audience.** A style that travels reaches people who would not have sought out either of its parents.

That last paragraph is the sort of thing that earns in Section B, where the mark scheme asks for a **critical argument** rather than a list. Say what the fusion *does*, not only what it contains.

rows: It mixes two types of music
It sets Punjabi dhol against a Western four on the floor bass drum
There are Indian instruments in it
The tumbi plays a repeated high pattern from the Punjabi folk tradition
The harmony does not really change
A drone rather than a chord sequence, so the rhythm carries the interest
A sampled string chord marks each eight-bar section, so the studio is a third ingredient
Neither tradition gives anything up: the drone needs no cadence and the loop needs none either

check.prompt: Which sentence would earn most in a question about how a fusion works?
options: The song combines traditional music with modern music in an interesting way
The pentatonic melody needs no cadence, so it sits easily over a loop that never resolves
There are instruments from two different countries playing in this track
The two styles go together well and it makes the track more enjoyable
check.solution: It names two features — a pentatonic melody and a non-resolving loop — and explains why they fit, which is a judgement supported by an observation. The other three make claims with no musical feature attached, so there is nothing for the knowledge half of the mark scheme to credit.

steps.title: Going deeper: fusion in the set works
steps.body:
Everything in this topic points at the two Fusions set works you meet in Year 10, so it is worth seeing where it lands.

**Afro Celt Sound System, *Release*.** Three traditions at once: West African, Celtic, and Western studio production. The West African side brings the **kora** and the **talking drum**; the Celtic side the **uilleann pipes**, the **bodhrán**, fiddle, whistle and accordion; the Western side loops, **reverb**, **delay** and hard-panned filtered synthesisers. All three are audible simultaneously, and that simultaneity is exactly what makes it a fusion rather than a medley.

**Esperanza Spalding, *Samba em Prelúdio*.** A **bossa nova**, and bossa nova is itself a fusion: Brazilian **samba** crossed with American **jazz**. The samba side brings the rhythm; the jazz side brings the harmony, which is far more complex than a folk style would use. It was one of the most popular Brazilian styles of the late 1950s and early 1960s.

Notice the pattern. In both, one tradition supplies the **rhythm** and another supplies the **harmony** or the **production**. That division of labour is extremely common, and spotting it is a fast route into an answer about an unfamiliar fusion.

**What a top answer does.**

- Names the traditions in the first sentence.
- Gives every feature a passport: *the kora, from West Africa*.
- Distinguishes a **drone** from a chord sequence and **heterophony** from polyphony.
- Treats the studio as an ingredient, not as packaging.
- Says what the fusion achieves, not only what it contains.
- Never writes "it mixes two types of music".

boxes.title: Say who does what

check.prompt: Bossa nova, the style of the set work Samba em Prelúdio, is itself a fusion. Of what?
options: Cuban dance music with American jazz
Punjabi folk with Western dance music
Jamaican dancehall with Latin American hip hop
Brazilian samba with American jazz
check.solution: **Bossa nova** is Brazilian **samba** crossed with American **jazz**: the samba side supplies the rhythm and the jazz side the harmony. Cuban dance music with jazz is Afro-Cuban jazz; Punjabi folk with Western dance is bhangra; dancehall with Latin American music and hip hop is reggaeton.

steps.title: What to carry forward
steps.body:
- A **fusion** brings two or more distinct traditions together **so that each remains audible**. Together, not in turn; audible, not absorbed.
- Name the **traditions** first, then give every feature a passport.
- **Bhangra**: Punjabi folk — **dhol**, **tumbi**, **chimta**, Punjabi vocals, call and response, pentatonic melody over a drone — set against Western pop and dance: **drum machine**, **synthesiser**, sampling, four on the floor.
- **Reggaeton**: Jamaican **dancehall**, Latin American music and **hip hop**. The **dembow** groups the 8 quavers of a bar as **3 + 3 + 2**, so one of its three accents falls off the beat and the whole pattern leans.
- **Bossa nova**: Brazilian **samba** with American **jazz**. **Afro-Cuban jazz**: Cuban dance music with jazz. **Jazz** itself began as a fusion of African and North American styles.
- **Drone**, **chord loop** and **ground bass** all replace changing harmony. Say which, and then say what it frees up.
- **Pentatonic**: five notes, no semitones, no pull towards a cadence.
- **Heterophony** is the same melody decorated differently; **call and response** is one phrase answered by another.
- The **studio** is a tradition in its own right: loops, sampling, reverb, delay, filtering.
- Say what the fusion **achieves**, not only what it contains.

questions.prompt: A synthesiser holds one low note under a whole track while the melody moves above it. What is that note called?

A ground bass
A drone

questions.prompt: Which traditions does reggaeton bring together?
options: Punjabi folk music and Western dance music
Brazilian samba and American jazz
Celtic folk music and West African music
Jamaican dancehall, Latin American music and hip hop

questions.prompt: The dembow rhythm groups the eight quavers of a four-four bar as 3 + 3 + 2. Why does that sound syncopated?
options: One of the three accents lands between two beats rather than on one
Because the three groups are of different lengths from each other
Because eight quavers cannot be divided evenly into three groups
Because the pattern repeats in every bar without ever changing
questions.solution: Counting the bar as 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &, the accents fall on quavers 1, 4, 7. The first and third land on beats; the middle one lands on an **off-beat**, which is the definition of syncopation. Unequal groups and exact repetition are both true of the pattern, but neither is what makes it syncopated.

markScheme.description: the middle accent falls off the beat

questions.prompt: Two parts play the same melody at the same time, one plain and one decorated with runs. Give the one-word term for this texture.
questions.solution: **Heterophony**: two or more parts playing the same melodic line simultaneously, with small variations between them. Polyphony would need the lines to be *different* melodies. Heterophony is common in fusions and rare in the Western classical set works, so hearing it is itself a clue.

markScheme.description: heterophony

questions.prompt: A melody uses only the notes G, A, B, D and E. What kind of scale is that?
options: Chromatic
Whole tone
Pentatonic
Harmonic minor
questions.solution: Five notes, and specifically degrees **1, 2, 3, 5 and 6** of G major, which is how the specification defines a **pentatonic** scale. There is no semitone step anywhere in it, so the melody has no leading note pulling to the tonic — which is exactly why pentatonic melodies sit so comfortably over a drone.

markScheme.description: pentatonic

questions.prompt: Which pairing gives the clearest evidence that a track is a fusion?
options: A dhol playing, then later a drum machine playing
Two dhols playing different patterns together
A dhol and a drum machine playing at the same time
A drum machine imitating the sound of a dhol
questions.solution: A fusion needs the traditions sounding **at once**, and the dhol and drum machine belong to different ones. Taking turns makes a medley; two dhols are one tradition twice; a machine imitating a dhol has replaced the tradition rather than joined it.

markScheme.description: both at the same time, from different traditions

questions.prompt: A solo voice sings a phrase and a group of voices answers it, over and over. Give the three-word term for this.
questions.solution: **Call and response**: a phrase in one part answered by a phrase in another. It belongs to **oral traditions** — music learnt by listening and repeating rather than from notation — and it turns up across West African, South Asian, Caribbean and gospel music, as well as in the blues.

markScheme.description: call and response

questions.prompt: Bossa nova, the style of the set work Samba em Prelúdio, is itself a fusion. Name the American style that supplies its harmony.
questions.solution: Bossa nova is Brazilian **samba** crossed with American **jazz**. The samba side supplies the rhythm and the jazz side the harmony, which is far richer than a folk style would use — added and extended chords, and modulations that a samba on its own would not attempt. That split, one tradition for rhythm and one for harmony, is very common in fusions.

markScheme.description: jazz

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you should take them when answering a question about an unfamiliar fusion.
items: Identify the percussion, which usually names one tradition at once
Name the two or three traditions the extract brings together
Attach each remaining feature to the tradition it comes from
Decide what holds the harmony still: a drone, a loop or an ostinato
Say what the fusion achieves that neither tradition could alone
questions.solution: Drums travel with their traditions and are the easiest thing to identify, so the percussion comes first and usually hands you a tradition for free. Naming the traditions comes next, because everything after it attaches to one of them. Then the remaining features, each with its passport. The harmony question follows, because in most fusions there is no chord progression to describe and saying "drone" saves you from writing about an absence. The judgement comes last: it needs everything above it on the table first.

markScheme.description: percussion identified before the traditions are named
traditions named before features are attached to them
the judgement about what the fusion achieves comes last

questions.prompt: An extract in A minor repeats the chords Am, F, C, G unchanged for its whole length. What effect does that have?
options: The harmony asks for no attention, so the rhythm and voice carry the interest
The music modulates repeatedly, so the tonality is unstable
Each repetition ends with a perfect cadence, giving a sense of finality
It makes the extract polyphonic, since several chords sound at once
questions.solution: Those four chords are **i, VI, III, VII** in A minor — one minor and three major — and they never change. A loop that never changes is deliberately unremarkable: it takes the harmony out of the conversation so the rhythm and the vocal can carry everything. Nothing modulates, no perfect cadence occurs, and chords sounding together make a texture homophonic rather than polyphonic.

markScheme.description: the harmony holds still so the rhythm and voice carry the interest

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT evidence that a track is a fusion?
options: A dhol and a sequenced bass drum are playing in the same bar
The track is unfamiliar and does not sound like Western classical music
A pentatonic melody sits over a drone while a sampled chord repeats
A kora decorates the same melody a tin whistle is playing plainly
questions.solution: Unfamiliarity is not evidence of anything. A fusion needs **two identifiable traditions sounding at once**, and the other three options each name two: Punjabi and Western studio, folk and studio, West African and Celtic. Judging a piece to be a fusion because it sounds foreign is the error this question is testing.

markScheme.description: the option that offers only unfamiliarity as evidence

questions.prompt: A dembow pattern groups the quavers of each four-four bar as 3 + 3 + 2 and repeats unchanged for sixteen bars. How many quavers pass in those sixteen bars?
questions.solution: Each bar holds 4 crotchets, and a crotchet is two quavers, so a bar is **8** quavers — which is exactly what 3 + 3 + 2 adds up to. Sixteen bars is 8 times 16, which is **128** quavers.

markScheme.description: 8 quavers a bar times 16 bars = 128

questions.prompt:
An extract from the Fusions area of study is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the vocal line and chord symbols above it.

**On the page:** no sharps or flats; four crotchets in a bar; a moderate tempo. The chord symbols above the vocal line read Am | F | C | G, repeating unchanged throughout.

**What you hear:**

- A sampled kick drum and rim-shot play a one-bar pattern whose accents fall in a 3 + 3 + 2 grouping of the eight quavers in the bar. The pattern never varies.
- Congas and a shaker add further layers over the same pattern.
- A rapped vocal in Spanish takes the first section; a sung vocal, heavily syncopated against the drums, takes the second.
- The two vocalists alternate two-bar phrases in the final section.
- A synthesiser bass doubles the kick drum exactly.
- A two-bar fragment of an older recording, clearly lifted rather than played, opens the track and returns between sections.

Explain how this extract is a fusion, naming the traditions it brings together and giving features from each.
questions.solution:
**The traditions.** This is reggaeton, and it brings together three: **Jamaican dancehall**, **Latin American** music, and North American **hip hop**. All three are audible at the same time rather than in turn, which is what makes it a fusion rather than a medley.

**From dancehall: the rhythm.** The sampled kick and rim play the **dembow**, the pattern that defines the style. Its accents group the 8 quavers of the bar as **3 + 3 + 2**, so counting the bar as 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & they land on quavers 1, 4, 7. The first and third are on beats; the middle one is between beats 2 and 3, so it is **off the beat** and the pattern is **syncopated**. Because it repeats without the smallest variation, that syncopation stops being a disturbance and becomes the pulse itself — the whole bar leans, and it leans the same way every time.

**From Latin America: the colour and the language.** **Congas** and a **shaker** layer further patterns over the dembow, and the vocals are in **Spanish**. The sung line is heavily **syncopated against the drums**, which is a Latin American habit rather than a hip hop one: the voice plays off the pattern instead of sitting on it. The two vocalists alternating two-bar phrases in the last section is **call and response**, which belongs to oral traditions rather than to notation.

**From hip hop: the production and the rapping.** The first section is **rapped**, and a two-bar fragment of an older recording opens the track and returns between sections — that is **sampling**, and the fact that the fragment is "lifted rather than played" is the evidence. The drums themselves are sampled rather than played, and the synthesiser bass **doubles the kick drum exactly**, which is a studio decision rather than a performance one: a bass player and a drummer cannot lock together that precisely.

**Harmony.** No sharps or flats, and the music settles on A, so the key is **A minor**. The chords read as **i, VI, III, VII** — one minor triad and three major ones — and they repeat unchanged for the entire extract. A loop that never changes is deliberately unremarkable. It takes the harmony out of the conversation so that every scrap of the listener's attention can go to the rhythm and the voices, which is exactly where this style puts its interest.

**What the fusion achieves.** Each tradition supplies something the others do not have and none of them has to give anything up. Dancehall supplies a rhythm strong enough to carry a track on its own; hip hop supplies a way of building records out of fragments; Latin America supplies the language, the percussion colour and a vocal style that thrives against a fixed pattern. A chord loop that never resolves would be a weakness in music that depended on harmony, and here it is a strength, because nothing in the extract is asking the harmony to do anything.

questions.prompt:
An extract from the Fusions area of study is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the whistle line only.

**On the page:** two sharps in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a fast tempo.

**What you hear:**

- A synthesiser sustains a low D and the A above it for the entire extract.
- A bodhran plays a rolling pattern with a double-ended beater; alongside it a djembe plays a different pattern with the hands.
- A tin whistle plays a four-bar melody that moves mostly by step and returns to D at the end of each phrase.
- A kora enters and plays the whistle's melody at the same time, decorating it with runs while the whistle keeps it plain.
- A bass drum on all four beats runs underneath from the halfway point onwards.
- Each phrase of the whistle is answered by a sung phrase from a solo voice, wordless.
- Reverb is audible on everything, and the whistle carries a delay that repeats its last note.

Analyse this extract as a fusion, referring to sonority, texture, tonality and the use of the studio.
questions.solution:
**The traditions.** Three: **Celtic**, **West African**, and **Western studio** production. All three sound at once.

**Sonority.** From the Celtic side, the **bodhrán** — a shallow frame drum played with a double-ended beater — and the **tin whistle**, which carries the melody. From West Africa, the **djembe**, a goblet-shaped hand drum, and the **kora**, a plucked harp-lute. From the Western studio, a **synthesiser** and a **bass drum** on all four beats. The two hand and frame drums are especially good evidence, because they are played completely differently — a beater against bare hands — so neither disappears into the other.

**Texture.** The most telling moment is the kora's entry. It plays **the same melody the whistle is playing**, decorating it with runs while the whistle keeps it plain. Two parts on one line with small variations between them is **heterophony**, not polyphony, and it is a texture that belongs to oral traditions far more than to the Western classical set works. Separately, each whistle phrase is answered by a wordless sung phrase, which is **call and response** — again from an oral tradition, where music is learnt by listening and repeating rather than from a score.

**Tonality.** The synthesiser sustains a low **D** and the **A** above it for the whole extract: a **drone** on tonic and dominant, a perfect fifth apart. Two sharps in the key signature and a melody that returns to D at the end of each phrase confirm the tonic. Because the drone never moves, there is **no functional harmony at all** — no progression, no cadence, nothing to resolve. The whistle melody moves mostly by step, which is **conjunct**, and a conjunct melody over a fixed drone can continue indefinitely without ever needing to arrive anywhere. That is the Celtic and West African habit, and it is precisely what allows a Western dance beat to be laid over it without a collision.

**The studio.** **Reverb** on everything and a **delay** that repeats the whistle's last note are studio effects, not performance techniques, and the **bass drum on all four beats** from the halfway point is Western dance music. These are not packaging. They are the third tradition, and the track would be a different piece without them: the four on the floor is what turns a tune over a drone into something with a floor under it.

**What the fusion achieves.** The division of labour is the point. The drone and the pentatonic-leaning, conjunct melody make no harmonic demands, so a relentless, unvarying dance beat can be placed underneath without fighting anything; and the two traditions' percussion sit in different registers and are struck differently, so the texture stays legible however many layers accumulate. Neither tradition is asked to behave like the other.

questions.prompt: The specification defines jazz as originally a fusion. Of what?
options: Brazilian and Cuban styles
African and North American styles
Punjabi and British styles
Jamaican and Puerto Rican styles
questions.solution: Appendix 3 of the specification defines jazz as "originally a fusion of African and North American styles", and notes that several varieties developed over time including New Orleans, swing and bebop. It is a useful reminder that a fusion which lasts long enough simply becomes a style.

markScheme.description: African and North American styles

questions.prompt: In a fusion, one tradition very often supplies one musical element and another supplies a different one. Which division is the commonest?
options: One supplies the melody, the other supplies the words
One supplies the rhythm, the other the harmony or the production
One supplies the loud sections, the other the quiet ones
One supplies the beginning, the other supplies the ending
questions.solution: Bossa nova takes its rhythm from samba and its harmony from jazz; bhangra takes its percussion from Punjabi folk and its production from Western dance; reggaeton takes its rhythm from dancehall and its production from hip hop. Spotting which tradition is doing which job is the fastest way into an answer about an unfamiliar fusion. The other three options describe a medley, not a fusion.

markScheme.description: rhythm from one, harmony or production from the other

questions.prompt:
A student writes this about a fusion extract:

> "This song mixes traditional music with modern music. There are instruments from another country in it as well as normal ones. It has a really strong beat that makes you want to move. The harmony does not change much which I think is a weakness. Overall it is a good mix of two types of music."

Explain what is wrong with this answer and rewrite it, using the extract described below.

An extract from the Fusions area of study is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the whistle line only.

**On the page:** two sharps in the key signature; four crotchets in a bar; a fast tempo.

**What you hear:**

- A synthesiser sustains a low D and the A above it for the entire extract.
- A bodhran plays a rolling pattern with a double-ended beater; alongside it a djembe plays a different pattern with the hands.
- A tin whistle plays a four-bar melody that moves mostly by step and returns to D at the end of each phrase.
- A kora enters and plays the whistle's melody at the same time, decorating it with runs while the whistle keeps it plain.
- A bass drum on all four beats runs underneath from the halfway point onwards.
- Each phrase of the whistle is answered by a sung phrase from a solo voice, wordless.
- Reverb is audible on everything, and the whistle carries a delay that repeats its last note.
questions.solution:
**What is wrong.**

**Neither tradition is named.** "Traditional music" and "modern music" are not traditions. A fusion answer is marked on the fusion, so every feature has to say where it comes from, and this answer cannot do that because it has nothing to attach features to.

**"Normal" instruments.** Calling the Western instruments normal and the others foreign treats one tradition as the default and the other as decoration. In a fusion both are ingredients, and an answer that only describes one of them has described half the music. It is also the reason nothing here is named: the answer never felt it had to.

**The harmony is misjudged.** "The harmony does not change much" is describing a **drone**, and a drone is a deliberate device, not a shortcoming. Music built over a held note is not failing to modulate; it has chosen not to have functional harmony at all, so that the melody and the rhythm can carry everything. Calling that a weakness is an appraising point resting on a misunderstanding of the observation underneath it.

**No feature is named anywhere.** "A really strong beat", "instruments from another country", "a good mix" — none of these can be credited, because there is nothing for a mark scheme to match. And the judgements have no observations supporting them, which is what an appraising point needs.

**Rewritten.**

> The extract fuses three traditions, all audible at once: **Celtic**, **West African** and **Western studio** production.
>
> From the Celtic side, a **bodhrán** played with a double-ended beater and a **tin whistle** carrying the melody. From West Africa, a **djembe** played with the hands and a **kora**. The two drums are struck completely differently, so neither disappears into the other.
>
> The texture is the clearest evidence of the fusion. When the kora enters it plays **the same melody as the whistle**, decorating it with runs while the whistle keeps it plain — **heterophony**, a texture common in oral traditions and rare in the classical set works. Each whistle phrase is then answered by a wordless voice, which is **call and response**.
>
> The synthesiser holds a low **D** and the **A** above it throughout: a **drone** on tonic and dominant. There is therefore no chord progression and no cadence anywhere, and that is a choice rather than a limitation — it is what lets a Western **four on the floor** bass drum be laid underneath from halfway without colliding with anything.
>
> **Reverb** on everything and a **delay** repeating the whistle's last note are studio effects, so the production is a third ingredient rather than packaging.

**Why the rewrite earns.** Every feature now carries the tradition it comes from, the Western elements are treated as a tradition rather than as the norm, the unchanging harmony is named as a drone and explained, and the judgement at the end rests on observations that were made first.

examTechnique.body:
**Fusions is one of Edexcel's four areas of study**, so an unfamiliar extract in Section A may well be a fusion, and the Section B comparison may pair one with a set work.

**Define it properly.** A fusion brings together two or more distinct styles or traditions so that each remains audible. Both halves matter: *together*, and *audible*.

**Name the traditions, then the features.** *This is a fusion of Punjabi folk with Western dance music: the dhol and the tumbi come from the first, the four on the floor bass drum and the synthesiser pads from the second.* That sentence is the whole shape of a good answer.

**Identify the percussion first.** Drums travel with their traditions and are the easiest thing to name.

**Watch for a drone.** Music built over a held note has no chord progression to describe. Say drone, and move on to what is happening above it.

**Listen for the texture.** **Heterophony** — the same melody decorated differently by two parts — is common in fusions and rare in the Western classical set works, so it is a signal in itself.

**The studio is often the third tradition.** Loops, sampling, reverb and filtering are Western studio practice, and in a fusion they count as an ingredient like any other.

**Do not call it a medley.** A medley plays one style and then another. A fusion has them at the same time.
examinerErrors: Saying a piece "mixes two types of music" without naming either of them.
Naming an instrument without saying which tradition it belongs to.
Calling a piece a fusion because it is unfamiliar, rather than because two traditions are audible at once.
Describing a drone as a chord, or complaining that the harmony does not move.
Missing the production entirely, when the loops and effects are one of the traditions in the fusion.
Confusing heterophony with polyphony, when the test is whether the parts play the same line or different ones.
Treating the Western element as the default and only describing the other one.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer names both traditions in its first sentence and then never makes a point without saying where the feature comes from. It identifies the percussion specifically — dhol rather than drums, congas rather than percussion — and knows that a held note under everything is a drone rather than a harmony. It treats the production as part of the fusion rather than as packaging, and it notices when the two traditions are doing the same job differently, which is where heterophony and call and response come from. And it can say what the fusion achieves that neither tradition could alone.
